Training LLMs for Multi-Step Tool Orchestration with
Constrained Data Synthesis and Graduated Rewards

Jiayang Cheng Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, HKUST, Hong Kong SAR, China Correspondence to: jchengaj@cse.ust.hk    Xin Liu Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA Correspondence to: xliucr@amazon.com    Zhihan Zhang Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Haoyang Wen Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Zixuan Zhang Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Qingyu Yin Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Shiyang Li Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Priyanka Nigam Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Bing Yin Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA    Chao Zhang Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA Affiliation: School of Computational Science and Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA    Yangqiu Song Affiliation: Stores Foundational AI, Amazon Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, HKUST, Hong Kong SAR, China
Abstract

Multi-step tool orchestration, where LLMs must invoke multiple dependent APIs in the correct order while propagating intermediate outputs, remains challenging. State-of-the-art models frequently fail on full sequence execution, with parameter value errors accounting for a significant portion of failures. Training models to handle such workflows faces two obstacles: existing environments focus on simple per-turn function calls with simulated data, and binary rewards provide no signal for partial correctness.

We present a framework addressing both challenges. First, we construct a reinforcement learning environment backed by a large-scale cache of real API responses, enabling a data synthesis pipeline that samples valid multi-step orchestration traces with controllable complexity and significantly higher generation efficiency than unconstrained methods. Second, we propose a graduated reward design that decomposes correctness into atomic validity (individual function call correctness at increasing granularity) and orchestration (correct tool sequencing with dependency respect). On ComplexFuncBench, our approach demonstrates substantial improvements in turn accuracy. Ablation studies confirm both reward components are essential: using either alone significantly degrades performance.

Keywords: 
Tool Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Function Calling, LLM Agents

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in using external tools through function calling (Patil et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2023). While significant progress has been made on single-step tool invocation, real-world applications often require multi-step tool orchestration, i.e., invoking a sequence of APIs in the correct order while propagating outputs from earlier calls as inputs to subsequent ones.

Recent benchmarks reveal that even state-of-the-art models struggle with multi-step orchestration. On ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025), which averages 3.26 steps per query, parameter value errors dominate failure modes (up to 78.8% for Qwen2.5-72B), indicating that models often select the correct function but fail to infer precise parameter values. Similarly, NESTFUL (Basu et al., 2025) reports that the best models achieve only 28% full sequence accuracy on nested function calls, with performance degrading sharply at depth ≥2\geq 2.

These findings suggest two key insights: (1) models need fine-grained feedback that rewards partial correctness rather than the standard all-or-nothing evaluation; and (2) training on multi-step workflows with explicit dependency handling is essential. Existing RL-based tool-use frameworks, such as ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025) and PARL-MT (Chai et al., 2025), primarily rely on terminal success signals or binary execution feedback. This sparsity is particularly problematic in orchestration tasks, where a single incorrect parameter in a multi-step sequence leads to total failure, providing no signal for the model to learn from partially correct reasoning paths.

Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to multi-step tool orchestration faces two fundamental obstacles. Challenge 1 concerns the lack of suitable training environments. While execution environments exist for tool learning (e.g., BFCL (Patil et al., 2025), tau-bench), they primarily target multi-user-turn scenarios with simple per-turn function calls rather than complex multi-step orchestration where a single user query requires multiple dependent API calls. Moreover, these environments often rely on simulated or synthetic data rather than real API responses, which can produce inconsistent dependency chains (e.g., a hotel ID returned in step 1 may not yield valid results when queried in step 2). Challenge 2 concerns sparse rewards. Standard binary rewards provide no learning signal for partial progress: a model that selects the right function but provides a slightly wrong date receives the same zero reward as one that calls a completely unrelated function. RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025) identifies this issue but focuses on reasoning tasks and has not yet been adapted for the specific constraints of multi-step tool use.

We present a systematic framework addressing both challenges (Figure 1):

  1. 1.

    Deterministic RL Training Environment with Constrained Data Synthesis. We construct a cache-based execution environment with 100k+ real API responses, ensuring consistent dependency chains across training iterations. Our constrained synthesis pipeline leverages workflow templates to achieve high generation success rates.

  2. 2.

    Graduated Reward Design. We decompose correctness into RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} (validating individual function calls at increasing granularity) and RorchR_{\text{orch}} (validating correct sequencing with dependency respect), providing dense learning signals for complex trajectories.

  3. 3.

    Empirical Validation. We evaluate in two settings: training on synthetic data to test generalization, and an oracle setting (training on in-domain evaluation queries) to establish an upper bound. RL training demonstrates substantial improvements in turn accuracy, and ablation studies confirm that both reward components are essential for success.

2 Methodology

2.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate multi-step tool orchestration as a sequential decision-making problem. Given a user query qq and a set of available tools ℱ\mathcal{F}, the agent must generate a sequence of actions 𝐲=(y1,…,yT)\mathbf{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}), where each action yt=(ft,𝜽t)y_{t}=(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}) consists of a function selection ft∈ℱf_{t}\in\mathcal{F} and parameter assignment 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}.

The execution environment is deterministic. Executing yty_{t} yields an observation ot=Exec​(ft,𝜽t)o_{t}=\text{Exec}(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}). Crucially, a subsequent action yt′y_{t^{\prime}} (where t′>tt^{\prime}>t) may possess a dependency on previous outputs. This is modeled as 𝜽t′←ϕ(o1:t′−1)\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t^{\prime}}\leftarrow\phi(o_{1:t^{\prime}-1}), where ϕ\phi represents the ground truth logic for extracting and propagating values (e.g., extracting a hotel_id to query room details). The agent must learn to approximate this dependency logic.

Our objective is to learn a policy πθ​(𝐲|q)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|q) that maximizes a reward R⁡(𝐲,𝐲∗)R(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{*}), where 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*} represents the ground truth workflow. Unlike standard generation tasks, validity is constrained by the underlying API logic: an action yty_{t} is valid if and only if all its dependencies are satisfied by the history Ht−1={(yk,ok)}k=1t−1H_{t-1}=\{(y_{k},o_{k})\}_{k=1}^{t-1}.

2.2 Deterministic Training Environment

Training LLMs for multi-step tool orchestration via RL requires a suitable execution environment. Existing approaches like BFCL (Patil et al., 2025) or τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024) often rely on simulated responses or lack complex intra-turn dependencies. We address this by constructing a deterministic environment grounded in real data. Our construction process follows three steps: defining workflow logic, collecting targeted data, and enabling constrained synthesis.

  • •

    Workflow Template Curation. Before collecting data, we must define valid orchestration patterns. We formalize recurring patterns as Workflow Templates that capture: ordered function sequences (f1,…,fT)(f_{1},\dots,f_{T}), dependency structures specifying how 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} depends on previous observations o<to_{<t}, and field paths for value extraction (implementing ϕ\phi). We curate over 100 templates spanning five domains (a concrete JSON example is provided in Appendix C).

  • •

    Workflow-Aware Cache Collection. To enable deterministic RL training without the latency and instability of live API calls, we build a cache-based environment that implements ot=Exec​(ft,𝜽t)o_{t}=\text{Exec}(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}). Crucially, we employ workflow-aware collection: rather than caching random independent API calls, we execute complete action sequences (y1,…,yT)(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) from the templates against live Booking.com APIs. This ensures that for every cached observation oto_{t}, the corresponding dependent observations ot+1,…o_{t+1},\dots that rely on values extracted from oto_{t} are also present.

    We collected 100k+ real API responses covering 40 functions in ℱ\mathcal{F}. Responses are indexed by hash of (f,𝜽)(f,\boldsymbol{\theta}), enabling O⁡(1)O(1) deterministic lookups. We implement comprehensive input validation with 8 specialized validators (date formats, coordinate ranges, enum values) to return structured error messages matching real API behavior.

  • •

    Constrained Data Synthesis. Rather than caching function responses independently, we execute complete workflow chains (workflow-aware cache expansion) to ensure cached responses form valid multi-step traces. The key insight is that freely exploring function chains leads to low data generation efficiency, as arbitrary combinations often violate dependency constraints or produce unsatisfiable parameter bindings. Instead, we use workflow templates (pre-validated on live APIs) as skeletons, then sample cache entries step-by-step following the dependency structure, and finally prompt an LLM to synthesize a query qq that would elicit the sampled action sequence {(ft,𝜽t)}t=1T\{(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}. The pipeline works as follows:

    (1) Reverse Index Construction. We build a three-level inverted index ℐ:(f,param,val)→{cache_ids}\mathcal{I}:(f,\text{param},\text{val})\to\{\text{cache\_ids}\}. For example, ℐ⁡(Search_Hotels,dest_id,"ABC123")\mathcal{I}(\texttt{Search\_Hotels},\texttt{dest\_id},\texttt{"ABC123"}) returns all cache entries where Search_Hotels was called with dest_id="ABC123".

    (2) Constraint-Aware Cache Sampling. For each workflow template, we sample action-observation pairs (yt,ot)(y_{t},o_{t}) step-by-step from the cache. Independent steps (no dependencies) sample 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} randomly from cached entries for ftf_{t}. Dependent steps use the reverse index: extract the required value from ot−1o_{t-1}, query the index, and intersect with other constraints to obtain valid 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}. If the intersection is empty (no compatible cache entries), sampling restarts from step 1 with different random choices. After a fixed number of retries, the current attempt is abandoned and a new workflow is sampled. This guarantees all successfully sampled entries form a valid ground truth sequence 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*}.

    (3) Query Generation. Given the sampled ground truth 𝐲∗={(ft,𝜽t)}t=1T\mathbf{y}^{*}=\{(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}, we prompt an LLM to generate a query qq that would elicit this action sequence. The prompt design prioritizes parameter fidelity over linguistic diversity: we instruct the model to incorporate all 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} values verbatim and require it to echo back the parameters in structured JSON format alongside qq. This echo-back mechanism enables automatic consistency verification between the natural language surface form and the underlying parameter bindings. We employ zero-shot prompting without few-shot exemplars, relying on the instruction-following capabilities of modern LLMs. The complete prompt template is provided in Appendix G.

    (4) Validation. We execute each yt∗=(ft,𝜽t)y_{t}^{*}=(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}) through the cache-based environment and verify: (a) cache hit for (ft,𝜽t)(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}), (b) successful execution yielding valid oto_{t}. Since parameters are sampled directly from cache, validation serves as a sanity check. Any step failure invalidates the entire (q,𝐲∗)(q,\mathbf{y}^{*}) pair.

The complete synthesis process is formalized in Algorithm 1.

2.3 Graduated Reward Design

The Sparse Reward Problem.

In multi-step tool orchestration, standard binary rewards (Success/Failure) fail to provide adequate learning signals. This failure stems from two factors. First, the combinatorial explosion of the action space: if a workflow requires TT steps and the probability of correctness at any step is p<1p<1, the probability of receiving a positive reward is pTp^{T}, which vanishes rapidly as TT increases. Second, the credit assignment ambiguity: a binary reward of 0 does not distinguish between a model that failed at step 1 (wrong tool) and a model that succeeded for T−1T-1 steps but failed at step TT due to a minor parameter typo. Without intermediate feedback, the agent faces a “needle in a haystack” optimization landscape where gradients are flat almost everywhere.

Two-Component Reward Structure.

We decompose correctness into two complementary components that capture different aspects:

  • •

    RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} evaluates each predicted action yt=(ft,𝜽t)y_{t}=(f_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}), i.e., whether the model generates syntactically and semantically valid function calls.

  • •

    RorchR_{\text{orch}} evaluates workflow completion against 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*}, i.e., whether all required steps are executed in the correct order with dependencies respected.

RatomicR_{\text{atomic}}: Atomic Validity.

For each predicted call, we assess correctness through two complementary validations:

Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Validation. We check syntactic correctness via three-level graduated scoring:

  • •

    Level 1 (α1\alpha_{1}): Correct function name

  • •

    Level 2 (α2\alpha_{2}): Correct parameter structure and types

  • •

    Level 3 (α3\alpha_{3}): Exact parameter value matching

For a predicted call y^=(f^,𝜽^)\hat{y}=(\hat{f},\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) matched against ground truth y∗=(f∗,𝜽∗)y^{*}=(f^{*},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}):

RAST​(y^,y∗)\displaystyle R_{\text{AST}}(\hat{y},y^{*}) =α1⋅𝟏[f^=f∗]+α2⋅sstruct(𝜽^,𝜽∗)\displaystyle=\alpha_{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{f}=f^{*}]+\alpha_{2}\cdot s_{\text{struct}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})
+α3⋅𝟏[𝜽^=𝜽∗]\displaystyle\quad+\alpha_{3}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}] (1)

where sstructs_{\text{struct}} measures parameter overlap and type accuracy (detailed definitions in Appendix B).

Semantic Validation. We execute the call through our deterministic environment and check for success: Rsem​(y^)=𝟏​[execution succeeds]R_{\text{sem}}(\hat{y})=\mathbf{1}[\text{execution succeeds}]. Concretely, we verify three conditions: (1) the call was executed and produced a response, (2) the response contains no error indicators (e.g., error fields or failure status), and (3) the response has valid structure (non-empty with expected data fields). Note that this is execution-based validation rather than output matching: we reward successful execution regardless of whether the returned data exactly matches ground truth. This catches errors that pass AST checks but fail at runtime (e.g., invalid date ranges, non-existent IDs).

Combined Score. AST and semantic validations are complementary: AST rewards structural correctness while semantic rewards functional correctness. We combine them equally and average over all KK predicted calls:

Ratomic=1K​∑k=1KRAST​(y^k)+Rsem​(y^k)2R_{\text{atomic}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{R_{\text{AST}}(\hat{y}_{k})+R_{\text{sem}}(\hat{y}_{k})}{2} (2)

RorchR_{\text{orch}}: Orchestration Consistency.

While RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} assesses local correctness, RorchR_{\text{orch}} enforces the global causal structure. Let 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) be the dependency graph of the ground truth workflow 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*}, where V={y1∗,…,yT∗}V=\{y_{1}^{*},\dots,y_{T}^{*}\} and an edge (j,i)∈E(j,i)\in E indicates that 𝜽i∗\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}^{*} depends on observation ojo_{j}.

We define a mapping function μ:V→{1,…,K}∪{∅}\mu:V\to\{1,\dots,K\}\cup\{\emptyset\} that aligns each ground truth action yi∗y_{i}^{*} to the index of the first matching call in the predicted sequence 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}}. A match requires the correct function name (parameter values are validated separately by RatomicR_{\text{atomic}}, enabling the two components to provide orthogonal learning signals).

The orchestration reward credits steps whose causal dependencies are satisfied:

Rorch=1|V|∑i∈V𝟏[i is matched]⋅∏(j,i)∈E𝟏[μ(j)<μ(i)]R_{\text{orch}}=\frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{i\in V}\mathbf{1}[i\text{ is matched}]\cdot\prod_{(j,i)\in E}\mathbf{1}[\mu(j)<\mu(i)] (3)

Here, 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. The term 𝟏[μ(j)<μ(i)]\mathbf{1}[\mu(j)<\mu(i)] ensures that dependency jj is not only executed but executed before the dependent step ii. The multiplicative product acts as a strict gate: a step receives zero orchestration credit if any of its prerequisites are missing or out of order, providing a strong gradient signal against causal violations.

The total reward combines both components:

Rtotal=λ⋅Ratomic+(1−λ)⋅RorchR_{\text{total}}=\lambda\cdot R_{\text{atomic}}+(1-\lambda)\cdot R_{\text{orch}} (4)

where λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] is a hyperparameter controlling the trade-off between atomic correctness and orchestration quality.

3 Experiments

We first validate that our cache-based RL environment provides effective learning signals (Section 3.2), then evaluate whether models trained on synthetic data can generalize to unseen queries (Section 3.3). We conduct ablation studies to understand the contribution of each reward component (Section 3.4) and analyze how performance scales with data quantity (Section 3.5). Finally, we examine which task characteristics benefit most from RL training through stratified and error analyses (Sections 3.6 and 3.8).

3.1 Setup

We evaluate on ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025), a benchmark specifically designed to assess multi-step tool orchestration. The benchmark comprises 1,000 test samples spanning five API domains (hotels, flights, car rentals, attractions, and taxis), with an average of 3.26 steps per query. We apply GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) for reinforcement learning using the verl framework (Sheng et al., 2024). We conduct training experiments on two base models: Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2024). Zero-shot refers to the original model without any task-specific training: the model receives a system prompt with tool descriptions and the user query, without in-context examples or fine-tuning.

Evaluation Metrics.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the evaluation set. For each sample i∈𝒟i\in\mathcal{D}, the ground truth sequence 𝐲∗(i)\mathbf{y}^{*(i)} is organized into N(i)N^{(i)} turns, where each turn contains one or more function calls (possibly parallel).

Turn Accuracy measures workflow completion progress by counting consecutive turns completed from the beginning:

Turn Acc=∑i∈𝒟Nsucc(i)∑i∈𝒟N(i)\text{Turn Acc}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}N_{\text{succ}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}N^{(i)}} (5)

where Nsucc(i)N_{\text{succ}}^{(i)} is the number of consecutive successful turns for sample ii. This metric reflects the cascading nature of multi-step orchestration: an early failure prevents all subsequent steps from succeeding. We also report Call Accuracy (proportion of correctly matched individual calls) as a secondary metric; detailed definitions are in Appendix D.

Training Configuration.

All experiments are conducted on 8×\timesH100 GPUs. We select batch size 16 and rollout size 16 based on preliminary experiments for stable training over extended steps. The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence coefficient is set to 0.001 (verl default), as we found it does not significantly affect performance. The reward weight λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 gives equal weighting to RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} and RorchR_{\text{orch}}.

3.2 Effectiveness of RL Training Environment

Before evaluating generalization, we first verify that our cache-based RL environment can effectively improve model performance. This requires isolating the effect of the execution environment from confounding factors such as distribution shift between training and test data.

Oracle Setting.

We design an “oracle” experiment where models are trained and evaluated on the same 100 queries sampled from ComplexFuncBench. This setup eliminates generalization requirements: if the model fails to improve, the issue lies with the RL environment or reward signal rather than data coverage. Conversely, substantial improvement validates that the environment provides useful learning signals. Note that baseline numbers in this section differ from Table 2 due to the smaller evaluation set.

Results.

Both models show substantial improvements through RL training (Table 1), with gains of 14–17% in turn accuracy. These results demonstrate that our deterministic cache-based environment provides the consistent feedback necessary for effective policy optimization. The improvement confirms that the graduated reward design (Ratomic+RorchR_{\text{atomic}}+R_{\text{orch}}) successfully guides the model toward correct multi-step orchestration. Subsequent experiments (Tables 2 and 4) evaluate whether these gains generalize to unseen queries.

3.3 Effectiveness of Constrained Data Synthesis

Having validated that the RL environment enables learning (Section 3.2), we now evaluate generalization: can models trained on synthetic data solve unseen queries?

Generalization Setting.

Unlike the oracle experiment, training and evaluation sets are now disjoint. We generate synthetic training data using the constrained synthesis pipeline (Section 2.2), varying the number of samples per workflow template (3 or 10). Models are evaluated on the full 1000-sample ComplexFuncBench test set. We compare three training strategies: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on ground-truth trajectories, GRPO with our graduated rewards, and SFT followed by GRPO.

Results.

Table 2 shows several observations: (1) SFT alone yields negligible gains or even degradation. Our error analysis (Table 5) reveals the root cause: SFT increases function selection errors at the sequence level (12.9%→\to28.3% samples stopped after function error) and worsens query parameter extraction (14.7%→\to15.8% error rate), suggesting that imitation learning on limited templates does not generalize well to novel query phrasings. Per-domain analysis (Table 7) corroborates this: SFT overfits to a subset of domains while degrading on others. (2) GRPO with fewer samples per template (GRPO-3) sometimes outperforms more samples (GRPO-10), though results vary across models and learning rates. (3) Qwen2.5-7B shows the largest gain with SFT+GRPO-3 combination (+13.7% over baseline). These results suggest that for strong base models, direct RL training may be more effective than SFT when data is scarce.

3.4 Reward Component Analysis

To understand the contribution of each reward component, we conduct ablation studies comparing RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} only, RorchR_{\text{orch}} only, and the combined reward.

Final Performance.

Table 3 shows that both components are essential. Using RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} alone yields the worst results (15.3% call accuracy), while RorchR_{\text{orch}} alone performs moderately (37.6% call accuracy). The combined reward substantially outperforms both, achieving 49.5% call accuracy.

Training Dynamics.

To understand why single-component rewards fail, we examine the training dynamics (Figure 2). Training with RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} only leads to orchestration collapse: the model achieves near-perfect individual call accuracy (Ratomic→0.97R_{\text{atomic}}\to 0.97) but loses the ability to coordinate multi-step sequences (Rorch→0.35R_{\text{orch}}\to 0.35). Conversely, RorchR_{\text{orch}} only leads to atomic collapse: the model completes workflows (Rorch→1.0R_{\text{orch}}\to 1.0) but generates low-quality calls (Ratomic→0.55R_{\text{atomic}}\to 0.55).

Mechanism of Atomic Collapse.

Figure 3 further dissects the atomic collapse phenomenon by breaking down RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} into its AST and semantic components. Under RorchR_{\text{orch}} only training, AST validity remains reasonable (∼\sim0.82), but semantic validity drops to ∼\sim0.45. This indicates the model learns to generate syntactically correct but semantically broken function calls—valid parameter names with invalid values that fail at execution. The combined reward avoids both failure modes by providing complementary learning signals: RorchR_{\text{orch}} guides tool selection and sequencing, while RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} ensures parameter correctness.

3.5 Scaling Analysis

How much synthetic data is needed for effective RL training? We investigate data efficiency by varying the number of samples generated per workflow template.

Setting.

Using our constrained synthesis pipeline, we generate training sets with varying density: 1, 3, 5, or 7 target samples per workflow template, yielding datasets of 67, 179, 283, and 383 samples respectively. All models are trained with GRPO using the combined reward and evaluated on the full test set.

Results.

Table 4 shows that performance plateaus quickly: increasing from 67 to 383 samples (a ∼\sim6×\times increase) yields no consistent improvement. This suggests high data efficiency—models capture workflow structural patterns from limited examples. However, this also indicates diminishing returns from sample density alone; expanding template diversity (the 40 templates that failed validation) may be more valuable than generating more samples per existing template.

3.6 Stratified Performance Analysis

Overall accuracy improvements do not reveal where RL training helps most. We stratify results by task complexity to understand which scenarios benefit from our approach.

Setting.

We analyze performance along two dimensions: (1) dependency depth—the longest chain of sequential function calls where each depends on previous outputs, and (2) dependency pattern—whether the workflow follows a linear chain or fans out into parallel branches. We compare three models: Zero-shot (no task-specific training), GRPO-3 (trained on synthetic data, disjoint from test), and RL-Oracle (trained on test queries, representing the upper bound).

Figure 4(a) shows performance by dependency depth. Both GRPO-3 and RL-Oracle improve over Zero-shot, with relative gains increasing at greater depths (+20% at depth 2, +31% at depth 4 for RL-Oracle). Figure 4(b) shows that fan-out patterns are harder than linear chains, but RL training helps consistently. Additional stratification by logical composition is in Appendix E.

3.7 Qualitative Analysis

To illustrate how RL training improves orchestration, Figure 5 examines a failure case in the parallel_conjunction category.

The baseline model fails to recognize that the query implies two independent search branches, stopping after the hotel search. This is not a parameter error but a structural one. The RL-trained model, penalized by RorchR_{\text{orch}} for partial coverage of the dependency graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, learns to execute all required sub-tasks.

3.8 Error Analysis

To understand where errors occur, we categorize failures at three levels: (1) call-level—among function calls the model produces, what fraction have incorrect function names vs. incorrect parameters; (2) parameter-level—among calls with correct function names, comparing errors in query-derived parameters vs. dependency-propagated parameters; and (3) sequence-level—whether the model completes the full workflow.

Table 5 reveals several insights. First, dependency propagation is not the primary bottleneck—dependency parameter errors (5–8%) are substantially lower than query parameter errors (13–16%), suggesting the harder challenge is extracting parameters from natural language rather than propagating values between calls. Second, “stopped after param error” is the dominant failure mode (22–28%); GRPO reduces all incomplete categories, with the largest improvement in “stopped after correct” (17.2%→\to12.7%), encouraging models to continue execution. Third, SFT increases function selection errors (12.9%→\to28.3%) while GRPO provides balanced improvements, suggesting imitation learning encourages more calls with lower accuracy, whereas RL improves both quality and completion.

4 Related Work

Tool Learning Benchmarks.

Early benchmarks primarily focused on API retrieval and single-step function calling. Recently, comprehensive evaluations like BFCL (Patil et al., 2025) and APIBench/Gorilla (Patil et al., 2024) have standardized tool-use assessment. However, these often target multi-turn conversational scenarios with simple per-turn calls. Our work specifically targets multi-step tool orchestration, where a single query necessitates complex, dependent API sequences. We evaluate on ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025), which identifies parameter value errors as the dominant failure mode—a finding that motivates our graduated reward design. Additionally, NESTFUL (Basu et al., 2025) and Seal-Tools (Wu et al., 2024) highlight the sharp performance degradation in nested function calls (depth ≥2\geq 2), further validating the need for the specialized dependency handling we propose.

Execution Environments.

Prior work addressed reproducibility through standardized evaluation (Patil et al., 2025), virtual API servers (Guo et al., 2024), and sandboxed environments (Yao et al., 2024), but these primarily target stable evaluation with synthetic or domain-limited data. We extend this philosophy to the training phase by constructing a deterministic, cache-based environment with 100k+ real responses, enabling the intensive trial-and-error exploration required for RL training on complex multi-step trajectories.

Training Data Generation.

Generating high-quality multi-step traces is a significant bottleneck. ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) utilized multi-agent simulation, while ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) scaled to 16k APIs. More recent approaches like APIGen-MT (Prabhakar et al., 2025) employ LLM committees for multi-stage verification. Our constrained data synthesis pipeline achieves comparable success rates using a single LLM call by leveraging workflow templates as structural skeletons.

Reinforcement Learning for Tool Use.

Standard RL approaches suffer from sparse, binary rewards. ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025) demonstrated PPO for single-step selection; ReTool (Feng et al., 2025) applied iterative fine-tuning but focused on math/code rather than API orchestration; RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025) and PARL-MT (Chai et al., 2025) identify the sparse reward issue but remain reliant on binary success signals. Our approach addresses this by introducing a graduated reward design, decomposing rewards into RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} (structural validity) and RorchR_{\text{orch}} (dependency fulfillment) to provide dense learning signals.

5 Conclusion

We presented a framework for training LLMs on multi-step tool orchestration: a deterministic cache-based environment with 100k+ real API responses, a workflow-aware data synthesis pipeline, and a graduated reward design combining RatomicR_{\text{atomic}} and RorchR_{\text{orch}}. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in turn accuracy, with ablations confirming both reward components are essential.

Impact Statement

This paper improves the reliability of LLMs in multi-step tool orchestration. As LLMs are integrated into autonomous agents executing real-world actions, ensuring they adhere to dependency constraints and parameter validity is crucial for safety. While our work reduces risks of incorrect API calls, autonomous agents carry inherent societal implications. Our constrained data synthesis and graduated rewards aim to provide more robust safeguards, contributing to safer agentic systems.

Appendix A Additional Training Analysis

This appendix provides additional training metrics that complement the main analysis in Section 3.

Figure 6 shows tool calling success metrics from a different perspective. The tool calling success rate (left) measures exact match with ground truth, while the executable rate (right) measures runtime success. Notably, RorchR_{\text{orch}} only training achieves only ∼\sim52% tool calling success despite ∼\sim90% executable rate, confirming that the model learns to generate different but executable calls rather than the correct ones.

Figure 7 demonstrates that the Combined model generalizes reasonably well, with validation metrics tracking training metrics throughout optimization. The gap between train and validation suggests opportunities for regularization or data augmentation in future work.

Appendix B Reward Computation Details

This section provides detailed definitions for the reward computation variables introduced in Section 2.3.

Notation.

For a predicted call y^=(f^,𝜽^)\hat{y}=(\hat{f},\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) and ground truth y∗=(f∗,𝜽∗)y^{*}=(f^{*},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}):

  • •

    Θ^=keys​(𝜽^)\hat{\Theta}=\text{keys}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}): the set of parameter names in the predicted call

  • •

    Θ∗=keys​(𝜽∗)\Theta^{*}=\text{keys}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}): the set of parameter names in the ground truth

  • •

    Θ^∩Θ∗\hat{\Theta}\cap\Theta^{*}: parameters present in both predicted and ground truth calls

Structure Score sstructs_{\text{struct}}.

The structure score measures how well the predicted parameters match the expected schema:

sstruct​(𝜽^,𝜽∗)=|Θ^∩Θ∗||Θ∗|⏟coverage⋅|type-correct||Θ^∩Θ∗|⏟type accuracys_{\text{struct}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})=\underbrace{\frac{|\hat{\Theta}\cap\Theta^{*}|}{|\Theta^{*}|}}_{\text{coverage}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{|\text{type-correct}|}{|\hat{\Theta}\cap\Theta^{*}|}}_{\text{type accuracy}} (6)

where:

  • •

    Coverage: fraction of required parameters that are present in the prediction

  • •

    Type accuracy: among overlapping parameters, the fraction with correct types (e.g., string vs. integer, list vs. scalar)

  • •

    |type-correct|=|{p∈Θ^∩Θ∗:type​(𝜽^​[p])=type​(𝜽∗​[p])}||\text{type-correct}|=|\{p\in\hat{\Theta}\cap\Theta^{*}:\text{type}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}[p])=\text{type}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}[p])\}|

Weight Values.

We use the following weights for graduated AST scoring:

  • •

    α1=1/3\alpha_{1}=1/3: function name correctness

  • •

    α2=1/3\alpha_{2}=1/3: parameter structure and type correctness

  • •

    α3=1/3\alpha_{3}=1/3: exact parameter value matching

These weights sum to 1.0, ensuring RAST∈[0,1]R_{\text{AST}}\in[0,1].

The following JSON structure illustrates a car rental workflow template with three steps and their dependency relationships:

The template specifies: (1) an ordered function sequence, (2) a dependency graph where step 1 depends on step 0 (for coordinates) and step 2 depends on step 1 (for vehicle ID), and (3) field paths for extracting values from previous observations.

Appendix D Evaluation Metrics Details

Call Accuracy.

This secondary metric measures the proportion of individual function calls that are correctly matched, regardless of turn boundaries:

Call Acc=∑i∈𝒟Kcorrect(i)∑i∈𝒟|𝐲∗(i)|\text{Call Acc}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}K_{\text{correct}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}|\mathbf{y}^{*(i)}|} (7)

where Kcorrect(i)K_{\text{correct}}^{(i)} counts matched calls and |𝐲∗(i)||\mathbf{y}^{*(i)}| is the total number of ground truth calls for sample ii.

Matching Criteria.

A predicted call y^=(f^,𝜽^)\hat{y}=(\hat{f},\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) matches ground truth y∗=(f∗,𝜽∗)y^{*}=(f^{*},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}) iff:

  • •

    f^=f∗\hat{f}=f^{*} (exact function name match)

  • •

    𝜽^=𝜽∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} (exact match on all parameter values)

This strict matching ensures that partial correctness (e.g., correct function but wrong parameters) is not credited.

Appendix E Stratified Analysis by Logical Composition

Among logical compositions, alternative_options (conditional branching) shows dramatic gains: GRPO-3 nearly doubles the Zero-shot baseline (43.7% vs 24.4%), with RL-Oracle reaching 48.1%. Interestingly, for fallback_logic, GRPO-3 (54.7%) slightly outperforms RL-Oracle (51.6%), suggesting that synthetic data training may generalize better for certain compositional patterns.

Appendix F Per-Domain Performance Analysis

Table 7 reveals domain-specific trends. Single-domain tasks (Attraction, Car-Rental) achieve 50–60% turn accuracy, while cross-domain orchestration remains challenging at 22–28%. Notably, SFT improves single-domain performance (Attraction: +8.1%, Car-Rental: +5.1%) but degrades cross-domain performance (27.6%→\to21.9%, −-5.7%), suggesting that SFT overfits to simpler patterns. In contrast, GRPO-3 maintains or improves performance across all domains.

Appendix G Prompt Templates

This section provides the prompt template used for query generation in our constrained data synthesis pipeline (Section 2).

The chosen_parameters field serves as an echo-back mechanism for automatic consistency verification between the generated query and the underlying parameter bindings.

This system prompt is used during both RL training (rollouts) and SFT. Tool schemas are injected separately via the tokenizer’s apply_chat_template(tools=...) parameter.

Appendix H Case Studies

This section presents case studies illustrating how RL training improves tool orchestration. Cases are selected where the baseline model fails but the RL-trained model succeeds.

H.1 Alternative Options (Conditional Logic)

The alternative_options category shows the largest improvement (24.4% →\to 48.1%). These tasks require handling conditional branches based on query results.

The baseline model uses an incorrect query format (“Tokyo anime” instead of “Anime, Tokyo”), causing the search to fail. The RL-trained model learns the correct parameter format through execution feedback.

H.2 Sequential Dependencies

Sequential dependency tasks require correct parameter propagation between steps. The baseline often fails to use outputs from previous calls correctly.

The RL-trained model correctly extracts and propagates the search_key parameter, demonstrating improved inter-call dependency handling.

H.3 Parallel Conjunction

Parallel conjunction tasks require executing multiple independent operations and combining results.

The baseline model completes only the hotel branch, missing the parallel attraction search. The RL-trained model learns to execute both branches of the conjunction.
